summary: The note explains how the 1881 assassination of President James A. Garfield by Charles Guiteau shifted civil service reform from a city-level concern to a leading national political issue. Guiteau had acted because he believed Garfield owed him a patronage job for his help in the 1880 election. After Garfield died two months later, Vice President Chester A. Arthur became president and pushed through civil reform legislation.
one_line: How the 1881 assassination of President James A. Garfield made civil service reform a leading national political issue, leading to Arthur's reform legislation.
key_facts: President James A. Garfield was shot in July 1881 by Charles Guiteau.
Charles Guiteau believed President Garfield owed him a patronage position for his "vital assistance" in securing Garfield's election the previous year.
Garfield died two months after being shot.
Vice President Chester A. Arthur acceded to the presidency after Garfield's death.
The assassination moved civil service reform from city organizations to a leading topic in the political realm.
Once in office, President Arthur pushed through legislation for civil reform.
Garfield's election occurred in 1880, the year before he was shot.
